                                        PROJECT NO. 58481

RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT ​ §                                 PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION §
STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561 §                                          OF TEXAS


     DATA CENTER COALITION’S COMMENTS ON THE DISCUSSION DRAFT


       The Data Center Coalition (DCC) appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments
to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) regarding Project No. 58481, Rulemaking to
Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards Under PURA §37.0561. DCC values the
Commission’s efforts to engage industry stakeholders in this important rulemaking process. DCC
offers the following comments on Project No. 58481 on staff’s proposed questions and
discussion draft.
                         I.​     Response to Commission Staff’s Questions


    1.​ Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load
       customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request? If so, how
       should the commission define those parameters?
​
​      The discussion draft states “A large load customer that is pursuing a substantially
similar interconnection request for electric service, the approval of which would result in the
customer materially changing, delaying, or withdrawing the interconnection request must
disclose the following information to the interconnecting electric utility.” Our members submit
interconnection requests because they expect to begin a new project. The approval of a
“substantially similar request” does not in itself signal that the large load customer will
withdraw another appearingly similar interconnection request. While requests may appear
duplicative, the industry may submit multiple interconnection requests to meet the significant
demand for data center services in Texas’s multiple markets and intend to complete more than
one project. At the same time, it should be noted that much of a project’s feasibility is often
outside of a company’s control as it pertains to their energization. If the Electric Reliability
Council of Texas (ERCOT) informs a company that they will not be energized for several

                               (DCC Comments on Project 58481– Staff’s Questions & Discussion Draft) 1
 years, the delay in energization may sidetrack the company’s plans – making the project no
longer commercially viable for its intended purpose. This is at no fault of the company. The
interconnection request may still come to fruition as it may be an opportunity for the company
to meet growing demand. This same logic holds for the rest of the United States. As stated in
PURA §37.0561 (d), the requirement to disclose similar or duplicative requests must be
restricted to projects within the State of Texas.1 Put simply, ERCOT should not consider the
presence of one interconnection request to preclude them from considering and approving
another request.

​           Further, DCC requests additional clarity on the definition of “substantially similar.” It
is our understanding that while SB 6 uses the terminology “substantially similar” that the spirit
of the law is to prevent duplicative requests as opposed to requests that may appear similar. As
mentioned, requests that seem similar may pertain to more than one project that a company
intends to complete. The current definition of a “substantially similar” request is one “which
would result in the customer materially changing, delaying, or withdrawing the interconnection
request.” Instead, this language could be used to define a “duplicative request.” While the
current language places the onus on large load customers to predict whether their plans may
change given various scenarios, the term “duplicative request” may better capture the goal of
SB 6 and offer regulatory clarity for companies to ensure they remain in compliance with the
law. Given the rule’s purpose is to ensure regulators are aware of duplicative requests within
Texas that may impact other energization requests, DCC offers the following suggested redlines
to focus the current language in §25.194. (c)(3) on such requests.



            §25.194. (c)(3) Proposed Language:

​       ​ (3) Substantially similar Duplicative interconnection request. A large load ​
​       ​ customer must disclose to the interconnecting electric utility whether the customer
​       ​ is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection duplicative request for electric ​
​       ​ service within the State of Texas, the approval of which would result in the ​
​       ​ customer materially changing, delaying, or withdrawing the interconnection request.

                    (A) A large load customer that is pursuing a substantially similar duplicative

            interconnection request for electric service, the approval of which would result in
           the customer materially changing, delaying, or withdrawing the interconnection
           request must disclose the following information to the interconnecting electric
           utility:

                      (i) the location, including the load zone, of the substantially similar
                      duplicative interconnection request;

                      (ii) the size of the substantially similar duplicative interconnection request;

                      (iii) the anticipated timing of energization of the substantially similar
                      duplicative interconnection request; and
                      (iiii) the interconnecting electric utility for the substantially similar
                      duplicative interconnection request.
           (B) A large load customer that discloses a substantially similar duplicative
           interconnection request under this subsection may anonymize competitively
           sensitive details in its disclosure to the interconnecting electric utility.
           (C) An interconnecting electric utility must not sell, share, or disclose
           information submitted to the utility under this subsection other than a disclosure
           to the commission or ERCOT.
           (D) The disclosure of a duplicative interconnection request does not preclude or
           alter the method of ERCOT’s consideration of a large load customers
           interconnection request.


2.​ Proposed subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the disclosure of specific
   information related to a substantially similar request for interconnection and
   allows a large load customer to anonymize competitively sensitive details. Should
   the commission list what is and is not competitively sensitive (e.g., load zone is not
   competitively sensitive information)? If so, what information should and should
   not be considered competitively sensitive such that the interconnecting utility and
   ERCOT can identify whether there is a duplicate request, or a request is unlikely
   to materialize?


                          (DCC Comments on Project 58481– Staff’s Questions & Discussion Draft) 3
          It is DCC’s understanding that this topic has been largely addressed by ERCOT’s
Protocol 3.2.7, which requires the anonymization of commercially sensitive information. The
Commission approved Protocol 3.2.7. on July 31, 2025.2 If the Commission believes that
additional language is necessary to assure the protection of commercially sensitive
information, DCC recommends that the Commission reference the below language in Protocol
3.2.7.

         Protocol 3.2.7 Language:

         (2) ERCOT must publish a Large Load Interconnection status report each month to the
         ERCOT website that aggregates Large Load Interconnection requests across multiple
         dimensions with as much specificity as possible while maintaining the confidentiality of
         Customer data, including:

                (a) Load Zone;

                (b) TSP;

                (c) Load type (as provided to the TSP, such as refinery, steel mill, data center,
                etc.);

                (d) Calendar quarter and year in which the interconnecting TSP submitted the
                project to ERCOT;

                (e) Requested energization quarter and year;

                (f) Size range;

                (g) Interconnection status (as defined by ERCOT to differentiate between
                operational, approved, under study, etc.); and

                (h) Co-location status.

         (3) ERCOT shall take actions such as providing ranges of interconnection MW sizes,
        aggregate loads, and other similar actions to protect, anonymize, and otherwise safeguard
        confidential and competitively-sensitive Customer data from public disclosure. When
        aggregating Customer data, ERCOT should ensure that at least five Customers exist in a
        particular Load type subcategory prior to aggregation, to protect against accidental
        disclosure. ERCOT may leave a certain category blank or aggregated with other Load
        types to avoid disclosure.

    3.​ Should the commission require a large load customer to notify the interconnecting
        electric utility and ERCOT of any change to information that is initially disclosed
        in response to this rule or only material changes to the information disclosed? If
        only material changes, how should "material change" be defined?
​
​        DCC recommends that large load customers only be required to disclose material
changes, which would be modifications that impact aspects of the load interconnection
agreement. Projects naturally evolve, but many details are unrelated to interconnection.
Limiting disclosures to material changes reduces administrative burden and promotes
efficiency by ensuring that ERCOT and the interconnecting utility focus on information
relevant to delivering energy and maintaining system reliability. Specifically, material changes
should only include modifications pertaining to interconnection such as location, MW size,
delivery date, and backup generation nameplate capacity. Information unrelated to securing
and delivering energy would create unnecessary compliance workload without improving
reliability.


    4.​ Proposed subsection (k)(1) authorizes an interconnecting electric utility to refund
        20% of a large load customer's security after energization and ratably as the large
        load customer meets the milestones identified in the customer's schedule for
        phased energization of its contracted load. Should the commission standardize the
        rate for refund for reaching milestones identified in the customer's schedule for
        phased energization (e.g., 20% for each year of operations until the full amount of
        security is refunded)? If so, how should the commission standardize the refund?
​

                           (DCC Comments on Project 58481– Staff’s Questions & Discussion Draft) 5
 ​         DCC encourages the Commission to structure rule language around achievement of
milestones rather than fixed time intervals. Milestones ensure that the agreements are focused
on completing projects. If projects are not moving forward, time is not the best measurement.



    5.​ Are changes to the commission's other substantive rules necessary to align with
        this rulemaking? If so, what changes need to be made to which rules?



​         DCC urges the Commission to maintain consistency in all language related to financial
commitments across rulemakings. Because financial security provisions also appear in the
criteria for inclusion in large load forecasting under Project No. 58480, DCC recommends that
the Commission align these requirements as each rule develops to ensure clarity and uniform
application.3

​         Further, the Commission should initiate an emergency rule to require that ERCOT
establish and maintain a queue based on the following criteria: (a) when the load request was
submitted, (b) a Transmission/Distribution Service Provider’s (TDSP) has an agreement and
meaningful deposit in place with the customer, (c) dynamic load modeling has been submitted
by a customer (d) a TDSP’s attestation that the load request and customer is real in their
estimation and (e) site control has been demonstrated by a customer. This process will promote
transparency and ensure companies can plan their projects by setting expectations for each
company’s rough timeline to energization.

​         Of note, the interconnection process is actively evolving, and ERCOT and PUCT
announced a new interconnection process at its open meeting on December 18, 2025. As such,
our recommendations may adapt as they continue to develop the new interconnection process.




3

                                   II. RECOMMENDATIONS


         DCC recognizes the intent of Project No. 58481, Rulemaking to Implement Large Load
Interconnection Standards Under PURA §37.0561, is to establish meaningful interconnection
standards and financial requirements that are scaled with the level of risk associated with a
project at a specific moment in the interconnection timeline. DCC agrees that financial
commitments should be reflective of risk throughout the interconnection process. However, DCC
believes the financial requirements must be founded in actual, quantifiable interconnection costs
paired with realistic, feasible timelines for providing financial security. At the same time, the
standards outlined within the rulemaking must reflect an accurate picture of a project’s
feasibility, with certain metrics like site control showcasing a more accurate picture of a project’s
long-term likelihood than certain regulatory approvals such as permitting progress. To reflect
these best practices, DCC offers the following recommendations to refine the process the
Commission has detailed in Project No. 58481.


End-Use Customer – §25.194. (b)(4)


       Multi-tenant data centers are data centers that contract with multiple clients to offer them
server space. To ensure clarity, DCC recommends that end-use customers be defined as follows
to account for data centers that serve as hosts of servers for multiple clients.


       §25.194. (b)(4) Proposed Language:

       §25.194. (b)(4) End -use customer - the legal entity that eventually will consume the
       electricity for its operations at the site subject to an interconnection request contracts
       with the TDSP for interconnection.


Project Developer – §25.194. (b)(10)


​      DCC understands that the intent of the project developer definition is to distinguish
between entities developing a project and those that are the end user. However, many
companies in the data center industry, including those within DCC’s membership, serve as

                            (DCC Comments on Project 58481– Staff’s Questions & Discussion Draft) 7
 both the developer and the end user. To reflect this reality, DCC proposes the following
language.


​      §25.194. (b)(10) Proposed Language:

       §25.194. (b)(10) Project developer -- An entity that develops a real estate site and
       owns the interconnection agreement. that is the end-use customer as defined in this
       section.


Requested Peak Demand – §25.194. (b)(11)
​

​       DCC encourages the Commission to clarify that references to “peak demand” indicate
either a percentage of the requested capacity or a stated peak specified in the facility’s
extension agreement that must be achieved.


       §25.194. (b)(11) Requested peak demand -- the total peak demand is the percentage
       of requested capacity that a large load customer requests, prior to executing and
       securitizing a discretionary services agreement, intermediate agreement, or
       interconnection agreement, that an interconnecting electric utility serves.


Backup Generating Facilities – §25.194. (c)(5)


       The current language requires the disclosure of information on a large load customer’s
backup generating facilities, including the number of units, nameplate capacity, fuel source,
operational characteristics, and the time required for each unit to begin serving the load. DCC
members recognize the importance of providing backup generator information so that
interconnecting utilities can plan for long-term reliability. However, details such as the number
of units, fuel source, and operational capabilities are subject to change—for example, when a
company purchases new equipment or changes providers. Therefore, the rule should allow
flexibility in the level of detail required, ensuring the focus remains on reliability while
minimizing the risk of outdated information. In this context, nameplate capacity is likely the



                            (DCC Comments on Project 58481– Staff’s Questions & Discussion Draft) 8
 most critical data point.


        Proposed Language §25.194. (c)(5):

        §25.194. (c)(5) Backup generating facilities. A large load customer must disclose to the
        interconnecting electric utility whether the customer plans to have on-site backup
        generating facilities. If the large load customer plans to have on-site backup generating
        facilities, the large load customer must also disclose the following information: the total
        nameplate capacity of the backup generating facility.

                 (A) the number of backup generating facilities;

                 (B) the nameplate capacity of each of the backup generating facilities;

                 (C) the fuel source and operational characteristics of each of the backup
                 generating facilities; and

                 (D) how quickly each of the large load customer' s backup generating facilities
                 can turn on to begin serving the load.



Site-Related Studies and Engineering Services – §25.194. (e)(4)
​
        DCC recognizes the intent of this section is to evaluate progress on site-related studies
and engineering services to better predict timelines and ensure large load customers utilize
their requested capacity. However, such progress is not always a reliable indicator of a
company’s commitment to completing a project. Numerous factors — many outside the
customer’s control — can delay these activities, making them an imperfect measure of project
viability.
        As mentioned in DCC’s previous comments on the criteria for large load forecasting
rulemaking (Project 58480), the timing of site-related studies and engineering services vary
considerably among large load customers.4 Currently, energy infrastructure requirements
4
 Data Center Coalition, Data Center Coalition’s Comments on the Proposed Rule, Project 58480, Item no. 35, at
7–8. (Public Utility Commission of Texas Oct. 17, 2025) available at
https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/58480_35_1549419.PDF


                               (DCC Comments on Project 58481– Staff’s Questions & Discussion Draft) 9
 require the longest lead time and are addressed early in the process, meaning that water,
wastewater, or gas studies or engineering services may have not yet commenced when large
load customers request load studies. Further, many projects would be considered to be
well-established projects before a number of site-related studies and engineering services
would be required. Because of this, DCC recommends the Commission strike subsection
(e)(4) in its entirety.


State and Local Regulatory Approvals – §25.194. (e)(5)


        As noted in DCC’s previous comments on large load forecasting criteria (Project
58480), permitting progress varies significantly across regulatory agencies with local and state
governments imposing different approval requirements and timelines.5 Additionally, permits
are often site-specific, and not all data centers require the same set of approvals. In many
cases, sites would be considered to be well-established projects before certain state and
regulatory approvals have made substantial progress. As such, DCC recommends the
Commission strike subsection (e)(5) in its entirety.


Backup Generating Facilities – §25.194. (e)(7)
​
        DCC offers the same comments as outlined in the section above on “Backup generating
facilities §25.194. (c)(5).”


Financial Security on a Dollar Per MW Basis. – §25.194. (e)(8)


        The discussion draft includes requirements for large load customers to provide
financial security at multiple stages of the interconnection process. DCC recognizes that these
securities, paired with the required disclosures, are intended to ensure that only vetted, likely
projects advance through the review process. While DCC supports the concept of tiered
financial security, we believe the rule could be improved to better reflect actual project costs,

5
 Data Center Coalition, Data Center Coalition’s Comments on the Proposed Rule, Project 58480, Item no. 35, at
7–8. (Public Utility Commission of Texas Oct. 17, 2025) available at
https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/58480_35_1549419.PDF


                             (DCC Comments on Project 58481– Staff’s Questions & Discussion Draft) 10
 allow unused payments to offset future security requirements, and establish more practical
timelines.
       First, DCC recommends that the security outlined in this subsection be applied as a
credit toward requirements in subsection (h)(8) and the CIAC payment in subsection (h)(9).
Without flexibility, these financial commitments could lead to significant over securitization.
If additional capital is needed for an Intermediate Agreement, DSA security, or CIAC
payment, the incremental amount can be billed at the appropriate time, with the security
provided under subsection (e)(8) credited against that amount. This approach ensures that
financial security requirements remain balanced throughout the process.
       Additionally, DCC notes that the proposed $50,000 per megawatt requirement
represents a substantial upfront security early in the process, when large load customers still
face significant uncertainty regarding project timing and costs with the TDSP. To better
balance the risk and cost at this stage, we recommend setting the initial security at $20,000 per
MW of contracted peak demand.
       DCC also highlights that if a large load customer has an existing discretionary service
agreement of at least $10,000,000 with the appropriate interconnecting utility, they should be
exempt from these requirements. Customers that have submitted the necessary Dynamic Load
Modeling, executed an intermediate agreement and/or discretionary services agreement, and
securitized at least $10,000,000 with an interconnecting electric utility have demonstrated
sufficient commitment for their project to proceed. In such cases, financial considerations for
energization have already been addressed, and imposing new requirements would
unnecessarily delay projects that have complied with existing regulations. Re-studying these
projects would create delays on new future loads. We recommend that the process prioritize
projects based on the date of submission to ERCOT, the interconnecting utility’s level of
conviction, and compliance with the above listed criteria.
       Finally, we suggest including language that highlights that 100 percent of the financial
security is refundable if a customer withdraws their load request or study, unless the security
has been applied to the CIAC payments or discretionary service requirements.


       §25.194. (e)(8) Proposed Language:

       (8) Financial security on a dollar per MW basis. A large load customer must pay financial

                          (DCC Comments on Project 58481– Staff’s Questions & Discussion Draft) 11
 security to the interconnecting electric utility $50,000 $20,000 per :MW of contracted
peak demand.

   (A)​ Beginning in 2027, the commission will adjust the $50,000 20,000 value on
       January 1 of each calendar year.

       (i) The annual adjustment will be proportional to the third quarter percentage
       change in the national Consumer Price Index (CPI)published by the United
       States Department of Labor, Bureau of Labor Statistics.
       (ii) The executive director must designate a substitute index to be used as a
       reference for adjustments if the CPI becomes unavailable.

   (B)​The interconnecting electric utility may accept the following forms of payment
       for the financial security:

       (i) cash collateral;

        (ii) corporate or parental guaranty, only if the corporation or parent corporation
       has a credit rating equivalent of BBB-/Baa3 or higher from a recognized bond
       rating firm; or
       (iii) a letter of credit issued by a bank with a credit rating equivalent of
       BBB-/Baa3 or higher from a recognized bond rating firm.

   (C)​If a large load customer has an existing executed discretionary service agreement
       with an interconnecting electric utility and the large load customer has securitized
       at least $10,000,000 with the interconnecting electric utility, then §25.194. (e)(8)
       shall not apply.
   (D)​The excess security outlined in this section can be used to offset security
       requirements in (h)(8) and/or CIAC requirements in (h)(9).
   (E)​The financial security outlined in this section is 100 percent refundable less any
       costs incurred by the TDSP in the instance of a customer withdrawing their load
       request or study, unless the security has been applied to the CIAC payments or
       security for the discretionary services agreement.



                  (DCC Comments on Project 58481– Staff’s Questions & Discussion Draft) 12
 Notification of Additional Study – §25.194. (g)(4)


       To ensure there is adequate time to pay for the costs of an additional study, DCC
suggests that large load customers be allotted 30 days after being notified that an additional
study is necessary to pay the costs of a study or withdraw its interconnection request. As such,
DCC suggests the following change.


       §25.194. (g)(4) Proposed Language:

       (4) The interconnecting electric utility must inform the large load customer of the costs
       for the additional study. Within 10 30 days of being notified that additional study is
       necessary, the large load customer must either pay the costs for the additional study or
       withdraw its request for interconnection. Failure to pay the costs for the additional study
       within 10 30 days may be treated as a withdrawal of the interconnection request.

Intermediate Agreement – §25.194. (h)


       DCC recognizes the importance of financial securitizations in providing assurances for
energy providers. However, the current language outlines multiple security requirements at
different stages of interconnection—some occurring close together in time. As noted earlier in
these comments, DCC supports a tiered approach for financial commitments that reflects the
actual risks at each stage, which we understand may be the intent of this section. However, we
believe the initial per-megawatt security should be applied to later security requirements
before requiring additional payments.


       Under this proposal, a company must:
       1) pay a non-refundable study fee
       2) pay $50,000 per MW (DCC is proposing this shifts to $20,000 per MW of
       contracted peak demand,
       3) sign an intermediate agreement with an additional securitization.


       Per our recommendation, the $20,000 per MW security should be credited toward


                          (DCC Comments on Project 58481– Staff’s Questions & Discussion Draft) 13
 subsequent requirements, such as those in subsection (h)(8) and the CIAC payment in
subsection (h)(9) to avoid over-securitization.
       Additionally, large load customers are required to provide extensive financial security
without the assurance interconnection. As currently written, customers must complete all
steps, yet ERCOT is not obligated to accept the intermediate agreement. Our members are
committed to paying the full cost of service, but the current structure imposes significant
financial obligations without certainty of outcome. DCC believes a more balanced approach
that aligns securitization, CIAC payments, and timelines would better achieve the
Commission’s objectives.


Site Control – §25.194. (h)(2)


       DCC requests that the site control requirements under §25.194. (h)(2) mirror the site
control requirements in (c)(2) and (e)(2) of the discussion draft. Like the referenced
subsections, purchase options, lease agreements, and deeds should demonstrate site control.
This consistency will ensure large load customers have uniform requirements to be in
compliance with the rule.


       §25.194. (h)(2) Proposed Language:

       (2) Site control. A large load customer must demonstrate site control for the load location
       through provision of one of the following property interests to the interconnecting electric
       utility:

       (3) a signed and executed lease agreement for the load location that is valid through the
       year that the large load customer's contracted peak demand is expected to be reached; or

           (A)​A legally binding option to purchase or lease for the proposed load location
           (B)​A signed or executed lease agreement for the proposed load location; or
           (C)​A deed for the proposed load location.


Site-Related Studies and Engineering Services – §25.194. (h)(4)



                            (DCC Comments on Project 58481– Staff’s Questions & Discussion Draft) 14
 ​
        As mentioned in the above section on §25.194. (e)(4), progress on site-related studies
and engineering services are not always the best reflection of a project coming to fruition. By
the time site-related studies and engineering services have commenced, a project will often
have completed several milestones that strongly indicate it is likely to proceed. Therefore,
DCC suggests the Commission strike this subsection in its entirety.


State and Local Regulatory Approvals – §25.194. (h)(5)


        As highlighted above regarding §25.194. (e)(5), state and local regulatory requirements
vary significantly by jurisdiction. Not only do requirements differ, the timeframes for completing
certain steps also vary. A disclosure of a company’s “plans, expected timing, and current
progress for obtaining state and local regulatory approvals” may not accurately reflect a project’s
likelihood of completion. By the time regulatory approvals are completed, companies may have
already dedicated extensive resources in a community, signaling a long-term commitment. For
these reasons, DCC recommends that the Commission strike this subsection in its entirety.

Backup Generating Facilities §25.194. (h)(7)


        DCC offers the same comments as outlined in the section above on “Backup generating
facilities §25.194. (c)(5).”


Financial Security for Significant Equipment or Services – §25.194. (h)(8)


        DCC’s understanding is that this financial security is in addition to the $50,000 per MW
requirement outlined in §25.194. (e)(8). All security requirements in this rulemaking should
reflect the actual cost incurred by the interconnecting utility to provide service for a large load
project—whether for equipment or infrastructure—across all sections of this rule.
Contribution in Aid of Construction (CIAC) – §25.194. (h)(9)


        Sections A, B, and C outline requirements for customers to pay the interconnecting utility
for its expected costs to provide service, but they do not require the utility to justify those

                           (DCC Comments on Project 58481– Staff’s Questions & Discussion Draft) 15
 estimates. DCC recommends the Commission include a provision requiring the interconnecting
utility to provide reasonable detail on CIAC costs, including the total dollar amount and MW
allocation for pro-ration.

       Also, DCC suggests modifying §25.194 (h)(9)(D)(i)(2)(B) to require that any remaining
balance be refunded within 60 days. Further, portions of the CIAC should be refunded if
equipment or infrastructure can be used by another customer. As currently written, a customer
may pay a CIAC for a pro-rated share of capacity and ultimately subsidize transmission and
infrastructure costs for another customer if the initial request is withdrawn. To ensure costs are
appropriately distributed, customers should receive a refund for any portion of the CIAC that
exceeds the actual cost of service.

​      §25.194. (h)(9) Proposed Language:

       (9) Contribution in aid of construction (CIAC). Before the interconnecting electric utility
       begins construction of facilities to interconnect a large load customer, a large load
       customer must pay CIAC in an amount that is equal to the interconnecting electric
       utility's expected costs to interconnect the large load customer and that are directly
       attributable to interconnecting the large load customer.

       (A) Costs directly attributable to interconnecting the large load customer include all costs
       associated with one or more new transmission lines built to interconnect the large load
       customer to the existing transmission network, including substation upgrades associated
       with interconnecting the new large load customer.

       (B) Costs associated with system upgrades that would not be required but for the
       interconnecting large load customer are costs directly attributable to the interconnecting
       large load customer. Where a system upgrade is necessary to serve multiple large load
       customers, such system upgrade costs must be pro-rated among those large load
       customers based on the contracted peak demand of each of those customers.

        (C) For a large load customer that is interconnecting to an existing transmission asset,
        costs directly attributable to interconnecting the large load customer include a share of
        the original CIAC that another large load customer paid under this section. The share of


                             (DCC Comments on Project 58481– Staff’s Questions & Discussion Draft) 16
        original CIAC must be calculated based on remaining net book value of the associated
       costs as a fraction of the original book value of those costs, and further pro-rated based
       on the share of contracted peak demand of the new large load customer as a fraction of
       the aggregate contracted peak demand of all large load customers associated v-rith that
       transmission asset, including the new large load customer. CIAC payments under this
       subsection must be credited to the previous large load customers that contributed to the
       previous CIAC payments, on an asset by asset basis, in proportion to those previous
       payments.
       (D) The interconnecting electric utility may accept the following forms of payment for
       CIAC:

          (i) cash collateral;
